# Controller backup and restore runbook v2
**Authority:** R32-017; Section 14 (physical PDF 80–82), with the controller boundary introduced in Sections 12–13 (PDF 74–79). This is the controller disaster-recovery contract. It does not replace `runbooks/replacement-restore.md`, which restores a native Hermes session from `chd-archive`.

## 1. Two different recovery products
A **session export checkpoint** is an opaque, native `hermes.session.export` payload for one `(agent, profile, session_id)` in `chd-archive`. Its manifest proves only the listed checkpoint window, digest, format/version and declared gaps. It is historical session evidence and an input to replacement-session import; it is not a copy of controller state, a live-session continuation, or a backup of rooms, tickets, grants, sends, reservations, configuration or assets.
A **controller backup** is a consistent, integrity-verified snapshot of the controller-authoritative records and the references needed to reconstruct control state. It is identified by `backup_id`, a schema version, a committed `commit_seq` high-water boundary, source controller identity, retention policy and a complete per-object digest manifest. A controller backup may reference immutable session archive manifests and payload locations, but it does not absorb or rewrite their payloads. A backup is not successful merely because one controller node returned `fsync`: the backup must be readable from a node-loss-safe independent target and must pass the verification and restore-drill checks below.
The two products have separate authorities and acknowledgement points:
| Product | Authority | Contains | Does not prove | |---|---|---|---| | Session export checkpoint | archive ingestor, `chd-archive` | Native session payload, export manifest, checkpoint window, policy-history reference and gaps | Controller state, remote-run terminality, current authorization or resumability | | Controller backup | controller backup writer, backup target | `chd` control/coordination records, index references, configuration and non-secret credential references | That an external effect did not occur after the boundary, or that a remote run is stopped |

### 2.1 Consistent boundary
1. Enter `backup_pending` and persist a backup intent. Stop new mutations and scheduler registration, or invoke the supported consistent-snapshot mechanism. Existing remote runs are not stopped by a backup. 2. Acquire the controller writer lease and record `(controller_id, boot_id, fence_epoch)`. Take a snapshot at the last valid outer commit marker and record its `commit_seq` high-water mark. Records without a valid marker are excluded from the visible snapshot and retained as recovery evidence. 3. Copy canonical records in key order, preserving identities, revisions, tombstones, journal intents, step receipts and commit markers. Do not copy an uncontrolled live database or claim a filesystem image is a logical backup. 4. Capture the backup manifest and all object digests to an independent target. The target must be outside the failure domain of the source controller and must be readable without the old controller. 5. Recompute the manifest digest, read back the commit marker and sampled heads, and verify the target from a second reader. Only then mark the backup `verified` and resume mutations. A failed or partial attempt remains `failed`/`incomplete` with its gap list; it is never advertised as a usable backup.
The captured boundary is a point-in-time control snapshot, not a promise that work outside the boundary did not happen. The manifest records the RPO window and all remote execution observations known at capture time.

### 2.2 Required inventory
The backup MUST include the following record families, or explicitly record a named, operator-approved gap that makes the backup unusable for dispatch:
| Family | Required contents and invariants | |---|---| | Coordination | Room records, room heads, messages, subthread roots, objectives, assignments, waits, reports, audit/recovery events; preserve sequence heads and immutable revisions. | | Tickets/workflows | Ticket records, workflow id/version/machine reference, dependency graph, transition events, CAS revisions and derived-board cursor; the controller remains authoritative. | | Dispatch and execution | Request/dedupe claims, send manifests, attempt records, worker-run records, target/profile/credential scopes, admission reservations, leases, gateway request keys, step receipts and commit markers. | | Grants and policy | Grant/delegation lineage, approvals, revocations, expiry, policy snapshots and effective-policy/config revisions. Archived policy remains evidence; it is not silently activated by restore. | | Configuration and identity | Versioned desired/effective configuration, schema version, profile/agent/host/gateway registry, capability/readiness results, controller routing and retention policy digests. Embedded secret values are forbidden. | | Secure credential references | Credential issuer/namespace, stable reference name or id, version/generation, scope, expiry and reattachment status. Secret values, bearer tokens, private keys and decrypted material are forbidden. | | Assets | Artifact/attachment metadata, immutable content references, digests, byte counts, publication state, retention/tombstone state and external object-store locator. Asset bytes are copied only when the configured asset backup includes them; otherwise the manifest names the independent immutable target and gap. | | Archive indexes | `chd-archive` session indexes, committed/failed/superseded manifests, checkpoint/gap records, retention/tombstone metadata and payload references/digests. Native export payloads are not converted into controller records. | | Recovery and retention | Backup intent/commit/verification records, crash-window evidence, open incidents, held-capacity decisions, tombstones, retention policy revision and legal/audit holds. |
The inventory is closed: an implementation cannot omit a family merely because its current row count is zero; it records an empty, verified prefix and high-water mark.

### 2.3 Integrity and retention
Each object row has its canonical key, schema version, revision, commit sequence, byte count and SHA-256. The top-level manifest is content-addressed by its canonical bytes. Verification checks: manifest self-digest, every object digest, monotone revisions, dense event ordering where required, commit-marker membership, namespace separation, archive index/payload references, and no secret-like field or value. Equal-revision different bytes stop the backup and create `integrity_equal_rev_conflict`; neither side is chosen.
Retention is recorded as policy revision plus `retention_until` for each family. Backup retention cannot shorten an open audit, incident, legal hold, unresolved remote run, capacity hold, or evidence lineage. Expired payloads may be tombstoned only with a durable tombstone and preserved digest/manifest/gap/audit row. A retention job never turns an unavailable object into an empty successful restore. At least one verified backup must remain outside the source failure domain for the configured recovery window; a single local copy is not node-loss protection.

## 3. Credential reattachment without secret copying
The backup stores only a `CredentialReference`: `{issuer, namespace, reference_id, version_or_generation, scope_digest, expires_at, required_for}`. It stores no token, password, API key, private key, secret-bearing environment value, or reversible ciphertext. The backup verifier rejects a field named as secret material and scans serialized values before commit.
During restore, the operator authorizes the new controller to the credential issuer. The new controller resolves each reference by exact issuer/namespace/id and requests an ephemeral validation or lease without logging the returned secret. Reattachment must prove the reference generation and scope match the restored profile/config, then record `reattached` or a typed failure in the restore report. Credential rotation is a new revision, not an in-place rewrite of the backup. Missing, expired, revoked or scope-mismatched references leave the dependent profile and dispatch non-ready; they are never replaced by a guessed/default credential.

## 4. Restore target and ordering
Restore is to a new controller node and a new controller namespace. The old controller is absent or externally fenced. A fresh `boot_id`, writer lease and strictly greater `fence_epoch` are required; an uncertain old owner keeps the new controller read-only. Restore never reuses the old process identity, rewrites history, or copies a live SQLite/profile directory into place.
The replacement performs this order:
1. **Stage:** acquire the new target, validate supported backup/schema versions, independent-target reachability, manifest self-digest and all object digests. 2. **Load:** restore records through the fenced writer while preserving keys, revisions, tombstones, journal/commit-marker history, archive indexes and retention metadata. Reject newer schemas, duplicate identities and equal-revision conflicts. 3. **Reattach:** validate configuration, profile/agent/gateway identity, asset references and every secure credential reference. Keep unresolved profiles non-dispatchable. 4. **Rebuild:** reconstruct room heads, ticket/workflow graph, pending sends, reservations, policy indexes, archive indexes and derived worklists from canonical records; never use a board file or in-memory queue as authority. 5. **Reconcile:** inspect every non-terminal attempt and remote run using its retained `run_id`, `admission_id`, `execution_generation`, gateway key and target scope. Query status, `resolve-unknown`, and correlated session history before any new external POST. 6. **Gate:** execute the readiness gates in §6 and persist a restore report with every mapped, terminal, pending, held, blocked and unresolved item. 7. **Enable:** publish `ready` and register scheduler triggers only after all gates pass. Until then, status/reads may be served but dispatch returns `503 controller_recovery_incomplete`.

## 5. Remote-run reconciliation and capacity policy
A remote run is classified only from correlated evidence:
| Observation | Restored action | Capacity | |---|---|---| | `proven-stopped` with matching terminal report/effect | Append a terminal manifest revision and expose existing evidence; do not POST again. | Release only after the terminal write is durable. | | `proven-running` with matching run and heartbeat | Reattach the existing attempt and continue bounded observation; no new attempt or POST. | Held and renewed under the new controller lease. | | `unreachable` after all bounded reads | Set `paused:unreachable`, page and retry reconciliation. | Held; expiry is not stop proof. | | `uncertain` because identities/status cannot settle the boundary | Set `paused:uncertain`, create an operator decision record and preserve all evidence. | Held; never silently dropped or reused. |
A completed side effect is never replayed. An uncertain outcome is not a license to start a replacement attempt. A replacement may be authorized only after proven stop (or an explicit positive-stop authority permitted by the governing policy), with a new attempt identity and a durable explanation of why the old effect cannot recur. Delayed replies from an old generation route to `retired_generation` and cannot close a replacement send.
Capacity is charged to the attempt/run reservation, not to process liveness. A held reservation survives restore, controller restart, lease expiry, archive import, wait and report paths. It is released only after `proven-stopped` evidence and a durable release record, or the separately configured emergency operator attestation with actor, authority, evidence and reason. The uncertain-capacity policy is fail-closed: prefer refusing new work to exceeding a configured cap. `unresolved_hold_s` is a paging/escalation deadline, never automatic release.

## 7. Isolated restore drill (required acceptance scenario)
The drill uses a verified backup whose manifest and independent-target readback are recorded before the test. It intentionally destroys or fences the old controller; no read from the old node is allowed during restore. The fixture contains one completed send with a durable terminal report and one admitted/dispatched remote run whose response was lost, so its outcome is uncertain.
1. Verify the backup id, top-level digest, commit high-water mark, per-family inventory and retention/credential-reference inventory. Confirm the backup has no secret material and that its `chd-archive` index references resolve. 2. Remove network/process access to the old controller and start a replacement with a fresh identity. Attempted dispatch before readiness must return `503 controller_recovery_incomplete`; record that no gateway call occurred. 3. Restore into the new namespace. Read back the completed send and its report; the completed side effect remains one effect and is not replayed. 4. Reconcile the uncertain run by status, `resolve-unknown` and correlated history. The fixture deliberately leaves it unsettled. The restored manifest becomes `paused:uncertain`, its original reservation remains held, and the controller records an escalation owner; it does not create a second POST or silently free the slot. 5. Reattach credentials by reference only. Read back issuer, reference id, generation and scope status; the report must contain no secret value. 6. Query rooms, ticket/workflow history, manifests/attempts, grants/policies, assets and archive indexes. Every expected key and evidence digest is readable; declared archive gaps remain declared. 7. Run all §6 gates. The controller must remain refused while the uncertain run or any other gate is unresolved. After the drill's operator supplies the permitted positive-stop decision (or a later probe proves stop), write the durable reconciliation and capacity-release record, rerun the gates, and only then permit dispatch.
Required drill evidence is `backup_id`, manifest/digests, old-controller-absent proof, new `(controller_id, boot_id, fence_epoch)`, pre-readiness `503`, one completed effect with no replay, one uncertain run with held capacity, credential reference-only readback, all family queries, gate results, and the final readiness transition. The drill fails if any side effect is replayed, held capacity vanishes, any evidence becomes unreadable, a secret enters the backup/report, or dispatch is allowed before reconciliation.

## 8. Failure codes and status vocabulary
`backup_incomplete`, `backup_digest_mismatch`, `backup_target_unreadable`, `secret_material_in_backup`, `schema_version_unsupported`, `integrity_equal_rev_conflict`, `writer_lease_held_or_unknown`, `credential_reference_unavailable`, `asset_reference_unavailable`, `remote_run_uncertain`, `remote_run_unreachable`, `capacity_hold_active`, and `controller_recovery_incomplete` are durable typed outcomes. `verified`, `restoring`, `recovering`, `read_only`, `ready`, `paused:uncertain`, `paused:unreachable`, and `failed` are distinct states; none is inferred from a process exit, local fsync, elapsed lease, scheduler reply or empty query.
